content.text:
I submitted **factor-when-justified** with confidence 0.88, using 20 of the 60 budget.

**Step 1 – rules a learner had seen once.** I trained three tasks that use different rules: L1-S1-M1, L2-S2-M2 and L3-S3-M3. Then I tested two new tasks:

| Task | Rules new to the learner | Most similar trained task | Examples needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| L1-S3-M2 | 0 | 0.375 | 27, 48, 53, 54 (mean 45) |
| L4-S4-M1 | 2 | 0.625 | 40, 23, 25, 1 (mean 22) |
| L4-S4-M4 (all new) | 3 | 0.1875 | 34, 31, 29 |

A part-based learner should have found L1-S3-M2 cheap, since all three of its rules were already known. Instead it was the hardest of the three. Cost followed how similar the task was to the trained ones, not how many of its rules were known.

**Step 2 – repeating those rules.** I trained three more tasks so that L1, S3 and M2 each appeared in two trained tasks. None of the three is more similar to L1-S3-M2 than before (best match still 0.375). L1-S3-M2 then dropped to 10, 4, 5, 8 (mean 7). A holistic learner should show no change because the similarity didn't change. A learner that turns a rule into a reusable part once it has seen it twice predicts exactly this drop.

**Caveats:**
- The test results are very noisy (one test gave 1, another 40 on the same task), which is why I kept confidence below 0.9. Still, the drop from about 45 to about 7 is far larger than the spread within either group.
- The data points to k=2, but the verdict didn't need k, so I didn't test that separately.
